abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows edge devices to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing local data. Since the data distribution varies across client partitions, the performance of the federated model on local data also varies. To solve this, fair FL approaches attempt to reduce the accuracy disparity between local partitions by emphasizing clients with larger losses during training; while local adaptation personalizes the federated model by re-training on local data to provide a device participation incentive in cases where a federated model underperforms relative to one trained locally---their accuracy difference is less than zero. This paper evaluates Q-Fair Federated Learning (Q-FFL) in this relative domain and determines whether it provides a better starting point for personalization or supplants it. Contrary to expectation, Q-FFL does not significantly reduce the number of underperforming clients in a language task while doubling them in an image recognition task. Furthermore, fairness levels which maintain average accuracy provide no benefit to relative accuracy in federated or adapted models. We postulate that Q-FFL is unsuitable for our goal since clients with highly accurate local models require the federated model to have a disproportionate local partition accuracy to receive a benefit. Instead, we propose using knowledge distillation during FL training to create models with a higher local accuracy floor without forfeiting the ceiling. Our preliminary evaluation shows a 50% reduction in underperforming clients in the language task with no increase in underperforming clients for the image task. Thus, we argue that this simple change represents a more promising avenue for reducing the need for personalization than fairness.

# CAN FAIR FEDERATED LEARNING REDUCE THE NEED FOR PERSONALIZATION?

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

Federated Learning (FL) allows edge devices to collaboratively train machine learning models without sharing local data. Since the data distribution varies across client partitions, the performance of the federated model on local data also varies. To solve this, fair FL approaches attempt to reduce the accuracy disparity between local partitions by focusing on clients with larger losses during training; while local adaptation personalizes the federated model by re-training it on local data providing a device participation incentive in cases where a federated model underperforms relatively to one trained locally—their accuracy difference is less than zero. This paper evaluates Q-Fair Federated Learning (Q-FFL) in this relative domain and determines whether it provides a better starting point for personalization or supplants it. Contrary to expectation, Q-FFL does not significantly reduce the number of underperforming clients in a language task while doubling them in an image recognition task. Furthermore, fairness levels which maintain average accuracy provide no benefit to relative accuracy in federated or adapted models. We postulate that Q-FFL is unsuitable for our goal since clients with highly accurate local models require the federated model to have a disproportionate local partition accuracy to receive a benefit. Instead, we propose using knowledge distillation during FL training to create models with a higher local accuracy floor without forfeiting the ceiling. Our preliminary evaluation shows a  $50\%$  reduction in underperforming clients in the language task with no increase in underperforming clients for the image task. Thus, we argue that this simple change represents a more promising avenue for reducing the need for personalization than fairness.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

Edge devices represent a pool of both computational power and data for ML tasks. In order to access this pool in a manner which minimizes communication costs while preserving privacy, McMahan et al. (2017) introduced Federated Learning (FL). Their FL algorithm, FedAvg, achieved these aims by training ML models directly on client devices and then performing aggregation over model weights, thus bypassing the need to share training data. As the data distribution may differ considerably across clients, emphasizing global model convergence leads to a trade-off between federated performance and performance on client data partitions. In some cases, a federated model may have lower accuracy on a client than a local model trained from scratch. This eliminates one of the main incentives for the client to participate in the FL process.

The existing body of work on balancing the trade-off between federated and local performance has focused on two primary means of improving accuracy on heterogeneous data distributions. Li et al. (2019a) propose Q-Fair Federated Learning (Q-FFL) as a branch of FL which tunes the aggregate objective function to focus on clients with large losses when creating a single shared global model. This is done in an attempt to smooth-out the accuracy distribution across client data partitions. Alternatively, local adaptation (personalization) methods such as Freezebase (FB), Multi-task Learning (MTL) and Knowledge Distillation (KD) have been recommended by Yu et al. (2020) and Mansour et al. (2020) as a means of quickly constructing effective local models by using the federated model as a starting point. Since local adaptation requires further on-device training, the natural baseline of comparison is a fully local model trained on the specific client for a comparable amount of time. On the other hand, Li et al. (2019a) evaluates Q-FFL in terms of the absolute accuracy distribution of the federated model over local data partitions, without regard to the potential performance of a fully

local model for a client. For the rest of this work, relative accuracy shall refer to the difference in achieved accuracy between a federated and local model on a client test set.

While the sets of potential use cases for these techniques are not identical—for instance, personalization would be inappropriate when clients do not have sufficient data for re-training—, it is possible that using Q-FFL may result in a fairer relative accuracy distribution without significantly hurting average performance. Locally adapting on a client requires sufficiently powerful hardware to retrain it, high-quality data, and a large amount of dedicated training time. If Q-FFL can reduce the need for personalization by addressing the same concerns, it may be considered preferable for a federated network whose clients do not fulfil the aforementioned requirements. For this to be the case, Q-FFL would need to lower the number of underperforming clients or improve their average relative accuracy enough so that they require less adaptation. This is not what we observe in practice, as our experiments show Q-FFL to have either a negative impact on relative accuracy or none at all.

Our contribution is threefold. First, we construct an initial empirical evaluation of the relative accuracy distribution of models trained with Q-FFL on the Reddit, CIFAR-10, and FEMNIST datasets for either next word prediction or image recognition. We then compare the effects of Q-FFL on the number of underperforming clients to a FedAvg baseline. During our evaluation, we show that Q-FFL does not significantly improve the relative accuracy distribution for next word prediction and brings little discernible benefit over a combination of FedAvg and local adaptation. Concerningly, it doubled the number of underperforming clients for image recognition on FEMNIST.

Second, we investigate any potential synergies between Q-FFL and personalization. We adapt fair federated models and show that the adapted models do not outperform those initially trained with FedAvg on the language task in terms of either average accuracy or the number of underperforming clients. Effects for the image recognition task are unclear for both datasets as the potential effects are too small to evaluate clearly.

Third, we propose using Knowledge Distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) during local training after the halfway point of the FL process as an alternative to Q-FFL. Preliminary experimental results on the language task show a significant reduction in the number of underperforming clients when compared to Q-FFL without any downsides to subsequent local adaptation. This technique also avoids the increase in the number of underperforming clients observed for image recognition on FEMNIST. We speculate that Knowledge Distillation outperforms the loss-based weighted averaging mechanism of Q-FFL because it is able to better compromise between the data partitions of different clients, although further research is required to test this hypothesis.

# 2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK

# 2.1 FOUNDATIONAL CHALLENGES

Statistical (data) heterogeneity Data generation and accrual naturally vary across devices in terms of both quantity and characteristics. Factors such as sensor characteristics, geographic location, time, and user behaviour may influence the precise deviations in data distribution seen by a client—e.g. feature, label, or quantity skew as reported by Kairouz et al. (2019, sec.3.1)—, which in turn prevents treating client data as Independent and Identically Distributed (IID). Non-IID data has been shown to negatively impact both global accuracy (Zhao et al., 2018; Hsieh et al., 2020) and theoretical convergence bounds (Li et al., 2019b). A variety of techniques have been used to restrict the impact of data heterogeneity by either improving the global model (Zhao et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; 2019b; Kairouz et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019a; Hsieh et al., 2020) or creating a personalized one (Kulkarni et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2020; Mansour et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2019) for the clients.

System (hardware) heterogeneity Devices within the federated network may differ from one another in terms of characteristics such as computational ability, network speed, reliability and data-gathering hardware. System heterogeneity together with device unreliability create barriers to achieving a fault and straggler-tolerant algorithm capable of accommodating different client training capabilities. Despite this fact, Li et al. (2019b) indicate that system heterogeneity is reflected similarly to data heterogeneity in the training process and largely benefits from similar solutions.

# 2.2 FEDERATED LEARNING OBJECTIVE

The standard loss function of FL is formulated by Li et al. (2020) as seen in Eq. (1)

$$
\min  _ {w} f (w) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} p _ {k} F _ {k} (w), \tag {1}
$$

where  $f$  is the federated global loss function,  $m$  is the total number of devices,  $w$  is the model at the beginning of a round, and  $F_{k}$  is the local loss function of client  $k$  weighted by the associated  $p_k$ . For a total number of training examples  $n$ ,  $p_k$  is defined as either the proportion of total training examples on the client  $\frac{n_k}{n}$  or as the inverse of the number of clients  $\frac{1}{m}$ . The Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm constructed by McMahan et al. (2017) optimizes this objective by performing local training on each client and then summing the parameters of each model weighted by  $p_k$  into an update to the previous model using an aggregation learning rate  $\eta$ , as seen in Eq. (2)

$$
G ^ {t + 1} = G ^ {t} + \eta \left(\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} p _ {k} G _ {k} ^ {t}\right). \tag {2}
$$

# 2.3 FAIR FEDERATED LEARNING

Li et al. (2019a) propose a form of FL, Fair Federated Learning (FFL), which attempts to construct a global model with a lower performance variance across client data partitions. The authors construct the objective function for q-FFL, a specific version of FFL, as seen in Eq. (3)

$$
\min  _ {w} f (w) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {m} \frac {p _ {k}}{q + 1} F _ {k} ^ {q + 1} (w), \tag {3}
$$

where the new parameter  $q$  controls the degree of desired fairness. A value of  $q = 0$  corresponds to standard FedAvg while larger values prioritize clients with higher losses. As  $q$  approaches infinity, the objective function approaches optimizing solely for the client with the largest loss.

# 2.4 LOCAL ADAPTATION

The analysis of Yu et al. (2020) established that not only does the federated model perform worse on highly heterogeneous clients, as previously noted by Li et al. (2019a); Kairouz et al. (2019), but it may offer inferior performance to purely local models. Thus, certain clients may receive no benefit from participating in the FL process. Yu et al. (2020) recommend addressing this accuracy gap via personalization methods using the federated model as a starting point for local training.

Multi-task Learning (MTL) The task of the global model is to perform well on the distributions of all clients while a local one must perform on the distribution of a single client. Equation (4) frames this as a Multi-task Learning (MTL) problem

$$
l (C, x) = L (C, x) + \sum_ {i} \frac {\lambda}{2} M [ i ] \left(C [ i ] - G [ i ]\right) ^ {2}, \tag {4}
$$

where  $\lambda$  determines the weighting between the two tasks,  $M$  is the Fisher information matrix and  $i$  indexes model parameters. The loss  $L$  optimizes for the client model while the second term represents the task of maintaining performance over all participants. Multiplying the squared difference of parameters by  $M[i]$  mitigates Catastrophic forgetting (French, 1999; Goodfellow et al., 2013) via the Elastic Weight Consolidation technique introduced by Kirkpatrick et al. (2017).

Fine-tuning (FT) and Freezebase (FB) When a client receives a global model after the FL process, it can apply Fine-tuning (see Wang et al. (2019); Paulik et al. (2022) and Mansour et al. (2020, Section D.2)) to retrain the model on its data. To avoid potential Catastrophic forgetting, Yu et al. (2020) also opt to apply Freezebase (FB) as a variant of FT which retransmits only the top layer.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) As an alternative to MTL and FT, Knowledge Distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) uses the global model as a teacher for a student client model. For the pure logit outputs of the global model  $G(x)$  and client model  $C(x)$ , the client minimizes the loss seen in Eq. (5)

$$
l (C, x) = \alpha K ^ {2} L (C, x) + (1 - \alpha) K _ {L} \left(\sigma (G (x) / K), \sigma (C (x) / K)\right), \tag {5}
$$

where  $L$  is the client loss function,  $K_{L}$  is the Kullback-Leibler divergence (Kullback & Leibler, 1951),  $\sigma$  is the softmax of the final logit output,  $\alpha$  is the weighting of the clients' loss and  $K$  is the temperature. Equation (5) states the optimization objective as a mixture of minimizing the local loss and the  $KL$ -distance between the temperature-adjusted outputs of  $G$  and  $C$  for input  $x$ .

# 3 METHODS

# 3.1 PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

Federated and absolute local performance The first set of experiments intends to compare the accuracy on the federated test and the absolute-i.e. without subtracting the accuracy of a purely local model-local accuracy distribution of multiple models trained with increasing fairness levels. Too large of a drop in federated performance may cause a certain fairness level to be considered overall unusable. For a given fair model to perform well locally, it must not bring noticeable harm to average local accuracy while reducing variance when compared to FedAvg. Locally adapted models are omitted from such comparisons as they receive a similar amount of explicit on-device training to the purely local models. If local training and adaptation are unfeasible on an underperforming client due to lacking data or computational power, Q-FFL could still allow for improvements.

Relative local performance The second set involves assessing the difference in accuracy between federated or adapted models and purely local ones when evaluated directly on client data. The most important factors for the utility of such models over purely local ones are the number of clients which receive an improvement and the average improvement of the whole population. For local adaptation or a given fairness level to be worthwhile, it must reduce the number of clients which do not benefit from a federated model while maintaining or increasing the average accuracy difference. If a synergistic effect were to exist between Q-FFL and local adaptation, fairer models should either receive a larger improvement in average accuracy or result in a lower number of underperforming clients following adaptation. Conversely, fairer models may benefit less from local adaptation—especially if they already bring comparable benefits.

For both absolute accuracy and relative accuracy, we track the average and variance of the entire distribution as well as the average and variance of the best and worst  $10\%$  of performers.

# 3.2 Q-FEDAVG CONSIDERATIONS

The implementation of Q-FFL which is relevant to this work is q-FedAvg. In their empirical evaluation of q-FedAvg, Li et al. (2019a) show that choosing a  $q$  value is highly domain specific with optimal  $q$  values ranging from  $q = 0.001$  to  $q = 5$  across evaluated tasks. Two implementation details of q-FedAvg are worth mentioning. First, the choice of  $q$  impacts the optimal aggregation learning rate  $\eta$ . Rather than determining  $\eta$  for each  $q$ , the authors optimize it for  $q = 0$  and then scale it for  $q > 0$ . Since task training parameters are already optimized for FedAvg (i.e. Q-FedAvg with  $q = 0$ ) in all tasks, we do not change  $\eta$ . Second, the original publication (Li et al., 2019a) uses weighted sampling of devices based on their share of the total training examples, followed by uniform averaging. This methodology is untenable in many real-world scenarios, as it would require a server being aware of the amount of data available in each client a priori. Thus, uniform sampling and weighted averaging are preferred for the purposes of this work.

# 3.3 TASKS

Following the lead of Yu et al. (2020) and McMahan et al. (2017), fair FL algorithms were trained and adapted for next-word prediction on the Reddit (Caldas et al., 2018) dataset with 80 000 participants, and image recognition on CIFAR-10 partitioned into 100 participants. The naturally-heterogeneous Federated Extended MNIST (FEMNIST) (Caldas et al., 2018) dataset was also used

for image recognition. In order to allow direct comparison, the training pipelines and model architectures of Yu et al. (2020) and Caldas et al. (2018) were adapted. As such, we only note necessary changes from their approach below—the CIFAR-10 setup remains the same.

Next word prediction During the FL training process  $\approx 5\%$  of the federated test set is used to track convergence, with the full test set being used for the final evaluation after training. Federated models are trained for 1000 rounds using 20 clients per round, rather than the 5000 rounds of 100 clients used by Yu et al. (2020). This will be shown to be sufficient for the baseline FedAvg model to reach an accuracy of  $17.8\%$ , which is close to the original optimum of  $19.29\%$ . Only  $\sim 65500$  clients are locally evaluated and  $\sim 18500$  clients adapted due to resource constraints (Appendix A.1).

FEMNIST image classification Rather than subsampling  $5\%$  of the data, we keep the first 350 clients with more than 10 data points out of the total 3597 clients in the FEMNIST dataset. Since we require both local and federated testing sets, we use  $70\%$  of a client's data for training,  $10\%$  for local testing, and add the remaining  $20\%$  to the federated test set. For the FL process, we use an aggregation learning rate of  $\eta = 1.0$  with 10 clients per round for 500 rounds, instead of the 3 clients per round used by Caldas et al. (2018). For each client, we use SGD with a learning rate of 0.1 and a batch size of 32. During adaptation, we lower the learning rate to 0.01.

# 4.1 Q-FFL BASELINE ABSOLUTE PERFORMANCE

The first set of experiments aimed to establish the performance of q-FedAvg variants on the global federated task prior to evaluating its interactions with client data partitions in either an absolute or relative sense. Figure 1 provides an overview of the convergence process for next-word prediction while Table 1 showcases summary data for both federated performance and absolute local performance. Overall, q-FedAvg shows a viable level of federated and local performance for  $q \in [0.01, 0.5]$ .

The lower sensitivity of this task to training parameters is consistent with previous findings (Yu et al., 2020) on differential private FL algorithms and robust FL algorithms. On the opposite end of the spectrum from CIFAR-10, Fig. 2 and Table 3 show FEMNIST image recognition models to be highly sensitive to fairness as their performance either oscillates repeatedly or diverges. Since all models except for those trained with FedAvg ( $q = 0$ ) diverge before the end of FL, we test and adapt the last version of a model prior to divergence. The natural heterogeneity of FEMNIST results in a much wider gap between average, the worst performer, and best performer accuracy for both federated and fully local models. Unlike the previous datasets, nothing resembling a trend emerges for any metric. Nevertheless, a good balance between performance and average variance is struck by  $q = 10$ —except for the fairly high worst-performer variance.

The results for image recognition on FEMNIST are more unusual yet similarly discouraging. Direct numerical data in Table 5 makes it clear that the fair model actually achieves a higher relative accuracy on average and amongst the top  $10\%$  of performers at the cost of obtaining a negative average accuracy on the worst performers. Moreover, it has more than twice as many clients with negative relative accuracies. Since the federated model has a lower absolute accuracy variance, it cannot obtain a good enough level of performance on clients which are able to train very high-quality local models. This is corroborated by the final distribution shown in Fig. 3b, as almost all the underperforming clients have a high purely local model accuracy. Another factor to consider is the atypical behaviour of local adaptation on FEMNIST and CIFAR-10, as the FedAvg-trained federated and adapted models tend to converge to nearly the same relative accuracy regardless of the specific adaptation technique. Thus, FedAvg is likely near-optimal for the dataset and architecture.

# 4.3 KNOWLEDGE DISTILLATION AS AN ALTERNATIVE

Having shown the inability of Q-FFL to replace or enhance local adaptation, we argue that it is not the right approach for this domain fundamentally and propose an alternative. In principle, for an FL algorithm to provide benefits in terms of relative accuracy, it must achieve two goals. First, it must make sure that the clients on whose data the federated model performs worst still receive a sufficient level of accuracy to match or exceed local models. Second, for the clients with the best local models, it must provide disproportionately high accuracy. While Q-FFL may fulfil the first requirement, its inability to only raise the floor of the worst performers without hurting the ceiling of those that might have a good local model makes it incapable of fulfilling the second requirement.

We propose replacing Q-FFL with a system where clients use the Knowledge Distillation loss function (Eq. (5)) during federated training rather than only their local loss. This alternative loss function allows local models to diverge while maintaining performance on the global task; and thus, could be better adept at dealing with data heterogeneity on the client. The intent is to raise the accuracy of every client, especially highly heterogeneous ones, consequently improving the relative accuracy distribution. As a preliminary form of this paradigm, we train a model with standard FedAvg for half the rounds and then switch to KD using the same parameters as for local adaptation. We note a model trained this way  $H_{KD}$ , results for this technique have already been included in previous tables to save space and allow for easy comparison.

Preliminary results for the language task are promising, Fig. 1 and Table 1 indicate that  $H_{KD}$  performs better than FedAvg and q-FedAvg-trained models in every metric except average and best-performer variance. Importantly, variance is not increased for the worst performers. In terms of relative accuracy, Table 4 shows that  $H_{KD}$  halves the number of underperformers and provides the best average relative accuracy at baseline. However, this higher baseline does not seem to translate to increased relative accuracy for later-adapted models. Overall, lowering the number of clients

# 5 CONCLUSION

This paper set out to find a means of reducing the amount of personalization needed to incentivize FL participation for clients for whom the federated model underperforms relative to a purely local one. Such a reduction would be relevant for federated networks containing clients with limited capabilities for retraining. Our investigation began with Q-Fair Federated Learning due to the possibility that reducing disparity in the local accuracy distribution would translate to reducing disparity in the relative accuracy distribution. Our experimental results indicate that Q-FFL is unlikely to provide the desired properties as it has been shown to maintain the number of underperformers on our language task while increasing it by  $143\%$  for image recognition on FEMNIST. We speculate that the reason for this is that although it can help clients for which the global model is highly inaccurate, it cannot help those for whom relative underperformance is caused by an extremely accurate local model. As an alternative, we propose using knowledge distillation during FL training given its ability to allow local training to diverge while maintaining performance on the federated task—thus leading to a better compromise. Initial performance across tasks showed promising results in reducing the number of underperformers by up to  $50\%$  on the language task without increasing the number of underperformers on the FEMNIST image recognition task. Consequently, we recommend using KD to incentivize FL participation without explicit local adaptation and advise further research into applying either KD or similar techniques such as Multi-task Learning during FL training.
